nt: The author is using the term **sons** to mean “descendants.” (This verse seems intended to list five generations of Judah’s descendants in order to provide an introductory summary for verses 2–23.) If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The descendants of Judah]

Given the apparent purpose of this verse, many interpreters consider the name **Carmi** here to refer to the Caleb who was the son of Hezron and the father of Hur [2:18–19](../02/18.md). Carmi may be an alternative name for Caleb, like Chelubai in [2:9](../02/09.md), or it may be the result of a copyist’s mistake. Since no ancient manuscripts or versions have the name Caleb here, we encourage you to use the name Carmi in your translation, but you could explain the apparent purpose of this verse in a footnote.

nt: The expression **was honored** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Now people honored Jabez more than his brothers]

Since the book does not introduce **Jabez** in any other way, many interpreters understand the term **brothers** to refer to the sons of Helah listed in the two preceding verses. This would mean that Jabez was a descendant of Judah through Hezron. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could suggest this possible explanation in a footnote.
It might seem that the expression **called his name** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [named him]

The author assumes that readers will know, as the context also indicates, that the name **Jabez** means “he causes pain.” You could indicate this in a footnote if that would be helpful to your readers.

See the discussion of the term **saying** in the Introduction to 1 Chronicles. In contexts such as this, it introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this expression explicitly, here, in the next verse, or in the other instances in this book.

nt: אִם־בָּרֵ֨ךְ תְּבָרֲכֵ֜⁠נִי וְ⁠הִרְבִּ֤יתָ אֶת־גְּבוּלִ⁠י֙ וְ⁠הָיְתָ֤ה יָדְ⁠ךָ֙ עִמִּ֔⁠י וְ⁠עָשִׂ֥יתָ מֵּ⁠רָעָ֖ה לְ⁠בִלְתִּ֣י עָצְבִּ֑⁠י

Following the custom of his culture, Jabez is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the second part of this condition. Alternate translation: [If blessing, you would bless me, and you would enlarge my border, and your hand would be with me, and you would act not {in} harm, so as not to pain me, then I would praise you and always be thankful]

Jabez is repeating forms of the verb **bless** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [you would surely bless me]

Here the term **border** represents “territory.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my territory] or [my land holdings]

Here, **hand** represents the power of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and your power would be with me]

Jabez is using **would be with me** as a common expression of his culture to mean “would help me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you would use your power to help me]

The author is speaking as if what Jabez **asked** God to do were an object that God **brought** to him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And God did what he asked]

nt: The author is using **broad of two hands** as a common expression of his culture to mean that the land was open on both sides, in other words, it was not a valley confined within mountains. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [was an open plain]

The author is using the dual of the word “hand.” He is not using the number two and the plural of “hand.” Translate this number according to the conventions of your own language and culture. If your language has a dual form, it would be appropriate to use it here.
וְ⁠שֹׁקֶ֖טֶת וּ⁠שְׁלֵוָ֑ה כִּ֣י מִן־חָ֔ם הַ⁠יֹּשְׁבִ֥ים שָׁ֖ם לְ⁠פָנִֽים

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [and, since descendants of Ham had been living there before they came, it was quiet and peaceful]

The terms **quiet** and **peaceful** mean similar things. The author is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [very peaceful]

The author is using the expression **to their faces** to mean “before them” or “previous to their arrival.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [before they came]

nt: The expression **written** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And these men whose names appear in the list above came]

The author is using the term **days** to refer to a specific time, the time when **Hezekiah** was the king of Judah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [during the reign of Hezekiah]
See the discussion of the term “struck” in the introduction to 1 Chronicles. Alternate translation: [and they attacked]

Here, the **tents** of these descendants of Ham represent their entire “settlements.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [their settlements]

The author is using the term **found** in a way characteristic of his language and culture to mean that these **Meunites**, members of a different people group from the descendants of Ham, could be found in the valley of Gedor, that is, they were there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who were living among them]
See the discussion of the phrase **to this day** in the introduction to 1 Chronicles. Alternate translation: [And they devoted them, and those groups never lived there again]
